title: Who the creek belongs to
carry: the creator dwells in creation, so serve it
tomorrow: the next crew to show up is a church youth group. does Simran stay?

lines: THIS ISN'T SEVA, THIS IS CHORES.
cards: Saturday morning, and Simran is shin-deep in the creek behind the strip mall, hauling out a shopping cart with Maya. Her gloves are soaked. A coffee lid floats past her knee.
She snaps a photo for the family chat: this isn't seva, this is chores. A minute later Bebe sends a voice note, the chili plants rustling behind her. Puttar, who do you think you're cleaning for?
Simran stands there holding one end of the cart, and doesn't have an answer.

teach.h: AIR GURU, WATER FATHER, EARTH MOTHER.
teach.b: Bebe's answer is already in the Japji, in the salok that closes it on Ang 8. In paraphrase: air is the Guru, water is the father, and the earth is the great mother.
Day and night are the two nurses, and the whole world plays in their lap.

teach.h: THE CREEK IS FAMILY, NOT SCENERY.
teach.b: So in the Japji's picture, that creek isn't scenery. It's the father, running through the mother's lap, with all of us playing nearby.

Here's the line to tell a friend tonight: the morning prayer ends by calling the air a guru. Then there's Asa di Var, on Ang 469. Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, I am a sacrifice to your creation; you dwell within it.
If the Creator lives in the creation, then the creek is not just where the trash ended up. It's a place to serve.
Seva means work done for others with no wage and no audience: washing dishes in the langar, wiping shoes at the gurdwara door.
Seva for the earth stretches that same apron outward. Planting a tree, clearing a riverbank, picking up a stranger's wrapper.
Simran texts back one word: family? Bebe sends a thumbs up. Then Simran and Maya lift the cart onto the bank together.

how: Some gurdwaras and Sikh youth groups plant trees, clean parks and riverbanks, and run seva days for the earth alongside their langar and other service.

games.q: what does “seva for the earth” mean?
o: a prayer said only at the riverbank at dawn
a fine paid by people who pollute a river
selfless service given to the creation itself

games.q: the Japji's last salok — tap the pairs.

s: seva only counts inside the gurdwara walls
seva is work for others with no wage; it stretches to the creation, where Guru Nanak says the Creator dwells.
the Japji ends by calling the air a guru
the closing salok on Ang 8: air the Guru, water the father, earth the great mother.
cleaning a creek is chores, not seva, because nobody thanks you
no thanks and no wage is exactly how seva is meant to be done.

games.q: you're at a park cleanup and a friend says, 'this is the city's job, why are we doing it for free?' going by today, what's the best reply?
o: the earth is family in the Japji. serving it is seva, whoever's job it is.
you're right, we should send the city a bill for our time.
it's mostly for the photos; that's how you get more volunteers.
games.why: the Japji calls the earth the great mother, and Guru Nanak says the Creator dwells in creation. that makes the park a place to serve.

practice: Pour a glass of water, or look at whatever water is near you. Look at it for the whole sit: how clear it is, where it came from, the rain and rivers it passed through.
For two minutes, let it simply be what the salok calls it: the father.

wordCard.voice: Seva for the earth. Selfless service given to the creation itself, because the Creator dwells in it.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: seva, selfless service given with no wage and no audience.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: the creator dwells in creation, so serve it. The earth is the mother in the Japji's last lines. Day 1709, lifted out of the creek.

sources.ref: Ang 8, Japji, closing salok (pavan guru paani pitaa maataa dharat mahat), paraphrased
Ang 469, Asa di Var, salok of Guru Nanak (balihaari kudrat vasiaa), paraphrased
